title: How to Edit Text in a PDF Online: Change Words and Fonts in the Browser
description: Edit the text already in your PDF with ChooseTools. Click any text, rewrite it, and change its font, size and colour. Runs entirely in your browser, no upload, no watermark.

sections.heading: The PDF Is a Final Artifact Until It Isn't
paragraphs: PDFs are where documents go to settle: layouts locked, fonts embedded, pages final. But every so often the settlement needs revisiting — a typo in the title, a company name that changed, a version number that is out of date. A capable [pdf-editor:PDF editor] makes those late-stage corrections possible without returning to the source application.
Free editors historically were stripped down to nothing but annotation. ChooseTools reads the text already in your file and lets you rewrite it, then restyle it with a font of your choice.
Everything happens locally on your device, so confidential edits never travel anywhere.

sections.heading: How the Editor Reads Your File
paragraphs: The first thing the editor does is scan the whole document. Every page is opened, every piece of text is measured, and the result is listed as blocks you can click.
Where a PDF stored a line as separate words, the editor joins them back into one block, so you edit a sentence rather than hunting for a single word inside it.
Because that reading happens on your own machine, a long document takes only as long as your device needs, and the file itself is never uploaded.

sections.heading: Click a Block, Rewrite It
paragraphs: Click any block of text on the page and it becomes editable. Type the corrected wording, and the panel on the side updates to show exactly what that block now says.

The change is drawn onto the page straight away, so you see the result before saving. If your replacement is much longer than the text it replaces, the block is outlined in red — a warning that the new wording may run into whatever sits beside it.

A colour control sets what gets painted over the original text. White suits a normal page; on a tinted or coloured background, match the cover colour to the page so the replacement sits invisibly in place.

sections.heading: Changing the Font
paragraphs: The font menu offers the 14 faces built into the PDF format itself — Helvetica, Times, Courier and their bold, italic and mixed variants. They need no download and are available instantly.

Those built-in faces cover Latin characters only, which is a hard limit of the PDF format rather than of the tool. To write Arabic, Greek, Cyrillic, or any script the standard set cannot reach, upload your own font file in .ttf, .otf or .woff2 format.

An uploaded font is embedded into the output, so the text stays selectable and editable in any PDF reader afterwards. It is subset down to the glyphs actually used, which keeps the file from ballooning. The family name is read straight from the font, so the menu shows the real name rather than the file name.
For brand documents, upload the typeface the rest of the document already uses and a corrected sentence will match its neighbours.

sections.heading: Size, Weight, Colour and Alignment
paragraphs: Alongside the font you set the size, the text colour, bold and italic. Built-in faces switch to their real bold or italic variant when you ask for one.

An uploaded font cannot be slanted, because a PDF has no way to synthesise a slant. For that reason the italic control is disabled while an uploaded font is selected, rather than quietly drawing upright text and calling it italic. Bold still works: the weight is faked by overprinting, which is how most editors approximate it.

Alignment decides where the replacement sits inside the space the original occupied — flush to its start edge, centred, or pushed to its far edge. For right-to-left text the edges swap automatically, so Arabic and Hebrew stay on the correct side.

sections.heading: Finding the Text You Want
paragraphs: Documents run long, and scrolling page by page to find one date is tedious. The search box filters every block in the document, not just the page on screen, and shows how many of them matched.
Clicking a result jumps to the page it lives on and selects it. Edited blocks stay marked in the list, so at a glance you can see the full extent of your changes before exporting.
Undo and redo cover every change, with the usual Ctrl+Z and Ctrl+Y shortcuts, so a misclick on the wrong line costs nothing.

sections.heading: What Changes, and What Does Not
paragraphs: Being precise about this matters more than sounding capable. A PDF stores text as instructions to draw glyphs at coordinates. Rewriting those instructions in place is possible but fragile, and it is not what this tool does.

Instead, the editor covers the original text with a rectangle and draws your replacement on top, in the position, size and alignment you chose. Everything else on the page — images, rules, other paragraphs, the page background — is left exactly as it was, because the underlying content stream is never touched.

The original typeface of an edited block is not carried over automatically. That is the one genuine trade-off: choose a font that matches the surrounding text if the document is brand-sensitive. The upside is that you are not limited to whatever the file happened to embed, and you can restyle a block deliberately rather than inheriting an arbitrary substitution.

sections.heading: Pages Without Text
paragraphs: A PDF made from a scan of paper has no text layer at all — only pixels. There is nothing for the editor to read, and it says so plainly rather than presenting an empty page.

Those documents need optical character recognition first, which turns the image back into real text. Once that exists in the file, this editor can correct it. Scanned documents also inherit whatever mistakes the recognition made, which is exactly the kind of error worth fixing before a document is sent on.
For converting a scan into an editable file in one step rather than correcting it in place, [pdf-to-word:PDF to Word] runs the same recognition and hands you a document you can rework freely.

sections.heading: Private Editing for Unreleased Work
paragraphs: Unreleased pricing, proprietary drawings and undisclosed plans should not travel to a cloud editor. Local editing keeps them confined to your workspace.
No watermark, no account, no retention; identical on Windows, macOS, Linux and mobile.
Edit in confidence, share the approved result.

sections.heading: Editing as Part of the Final Polish
paragraphs: The common final pass pairs text corrections with [compress-pdf:compression], [watermark-pdf:watermarking] and [protect-pdf:encryption] before dispatch.
Page structure, rotation and extraction have their own tools: [rotate-pdf:rotating], [delete-pdf-pages:removing pages] and [reorder-pdf:reordering] cover those jobs without loading a full editor.
Free browser-based editing closes the gap between "nearly final" and "sent".

faqs.q: Can I change text inside an existing PDF?
faqs.a: Yes. Every page is scanned on your device and the text is listed as clickable blocks. Click one, type the new wording, and the change is written into the file you download.

faqs.q: Does editing require uploading my document?
faqs.a: No. Reading the file, applying your edits and producing the new PDF all run in your browser. The file never leaves your device, and there is no account or watermark involved.

faqs.q: What kinds of edits are supported?
faqs.a: Text. Click any block, rewrite it, and set its font, size, colour, weight, alignment and cover colour. Images, page structure and form fields are not editable here; use the dedicated tools for those.

faqs.q: Will correcting text damage the rest of the layout?
faqs.a: No. Only the block you edit is affected. The original text is covered with a rectangle and the replacement is drawn on top, so images, rules and neighbouring paragraphs are untouched. If your replacement is far longer than the text it replaces, the editor marks the block so you can shorten it or reduce the size before saving.

faqs.q: Can I use my own font?
faqs.a: Yes. Upload a .ttf, .otf or .woff2 file and it is embedded in the output, subset to the characters you actually used. This is the only way to write Arabic, because the 14 fonts built into the PDF format cover Latin characters only.

faqs.q: What happens to the original typeface?
faqs.a: It is not preserved automatically. An edited block is drawn in the font you choose, so for a document with strict branding, upload the matching typeface first. Everything on the page that you did not edit keeps its original font.
